abstract: Cetaceans reduce the net cost of sustained swimming through intermittent locomotion, alternating active fluking with unpowered gliding. The energy balance of this strategy is central to understanding survival rates, population sustainability, and the effects of anthropogenic and environmental pressures. While active-phase energetics have been characterized extensively, the glide phase remains largely unexplored. Here we derive the optimal glide duration (Topt) and the maximum glide duration beyond which energy savings vanish (Tzero) for three odontocetes spanning a 20-fold range in body mass, using high-fidelity CAD models and wall-modeled large eddy simulations. We show analytically that speed retention at Topt and mass-specific peak energy savings are both fully determined by the active-to-passive drag ratio, propulsive efficiency, and swimming speed, independently of body morphometry and drag coefficient, and are therefore invariant across species at any given speed. These passive-phase optima extend the known size-independent active-phase invariants to the glide phase, towards a scale-independent energetic framework for burst-and-glide locomotion in small cetaceans.
